authoredPrompt: This figure pairs two views of the same max-heap, labeled (a) on the left and (b) on the right. Panel (a) is a binary tree of ten gray circles joined by straight edges, with the value inside each circle and a smaller index printed just above and outside it. The root holds 16 at index 1; its children hold 14 at index 2 and 10 at index 3; the node 14 has children 8 at index 4 and 7 at index 5; the node 10 has children 9 at index 6 and 3 at index 7; the node 8 has children 2 at index 8 and 4 at index 9; and the node 7 has a single left child, 1 at index 10, so the bottom level is filled only from the left. Panel (b) is a horizontal row of ten gray boxes reading 16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1 from left to right, with the indices 1 through 10 written above them. Curved arcs above and below the row connect each cell to the two cells that hold its children, which always lie further right. Setting the branching picture beside the flat row shows that the same parent-child relationships survive the change of representation. The figure introduces the array form of a heap, in which moving between a node and its children reduces to arithmetic on the index.
authoredInteractions:
- Click for a tree node or array cell: the corresponding item in the other view highlights along with its parent and children, making clear that the tree and array store the same heap relationships.
- Slider for index i from 1 to 10: the display highlights floor(i/2), 2i, and 2i+1 when they exist, making clear how simple index arithmetic navigates from a node to its relatives.
- Toggle between value order and structural order overlays: max-heap comparisons or parent-child arcs are emphasized, making clear the difference between the heap property and the array layout.
authoredContext: The (binary) heap data structure is an array object that we can view as a nearly complete binary tree (see Section B.5.3), as shown in Figure 6.1. Each node of the tree corresponds to an element of the array. The tree is completely filled on all levels except possibly the lowest, which is filled from the left up to a point. An array A that represents a heap is an object with two attributes: A:length, which (as usual) gives the number of elements in the array, and A:heap-size, which represents how many elements in the heap are stored within array A. discrepancies: The heap tree and array panels are rendered much smaller within the available screenshot, with a large UI/control area beside them, so the default view is less like the source's full-width textbook figure.
The array-link arcs in panel (b) are less cleanly nested than in the source; several top arcs pass very close to or through the index-label area and the bottom arcs visually crowd together.

The generated figure adds interactive highlighting/overlay affordances and explanatory UI text that are not part of the source static figure, though the default graphic itself remains mostly unhighlighted.
evaluation.notes: The tree topology, array order, values, indices, gray fills, and panel labels are all essentially correct, but the rendered figure is undersized and the array arcs/labels are less faithful and clean than the source.
action_items: Scale the main SVG content up or move the control UI below/into a smaller dock so the two panels fill the horizontal space more like the source figure.
Refine the array arc paths so the top arcs sit cleanly above the index labels and the bottom arcs have clearer separation matching the textbook nesting.
Keep all overlay/highlight elements fully absent from the initial static view or make the initial UI state visually consistent with the unselected default.
